Mail Gateway Resilience After CVE-2026-113425


Mail infrastructure is easy to leave in a maintenance exception because it is always on and difficult to interrupt. CVE-2026-113425 gives teams a reason to revisit that habit. The NGINX mail proxy received a critical use-after-free fix, and the recovery plan around that component should be tested as carefully as the package update.
F5 assigned CVE-2026-113425 to a use-after-free in ngx_mail_proxy_module. The affected product configurations are NGINX Open Source and NGINX Plus running as mail proxies. A specially crafted mail session can cause worker termination, memory corruption, or potential code execution when ASLR is disabled or bypassable.
The vulnerability is CWE-416. F5 published the fix on November 18, 2026. The fixed NGINX Open Sourc…
articles.title: Mail Gateway Resilience After CVE-2026-113425

articles.author: Aaron Sun
articles.description:
AI disclosure: this post was written with the help of Claude Code.
I'm a dad and a developer in Sweden. Over the last months I've been building small tools and games that scratch my own itches, and I finally put them all on one page: https://zexa.se/?ref=devto
I built most of this with a lot of help from Claude Code, and I say so on every page. Everything is free, with no ads.
Zexa Timer: a stage and classroom countdown. Show it on any screen, control it from your phone. No sign-up.
Nordic Dual Subs: a Chrome extension that shows Swedish/Norwegian/Danish subtitles plus a translation at the same time on SVT Play, UR, NRK and DR.
Melarka: a self-hosted music server for the family. It's my Spotify replacement in the car. Open source.
Pullbell, Hopback and Tabrelay: open-source menu-bar and Chrome tools for people who live in GitHub and Claude Code.
senote.se: a site for Chinese speakers in Sweden.
Egg Raiders and Brick Smash: kid-friendly Roblox games.
Each project has its own subdomain, but nobody remembers nine URLs. The home page is just a list with a sentence each, plus the structured data search engines like. Keeping every project on its own subdomain also means one can fail or get retired without touching the others.
A small honest story ("I wanted this myself") gets more reaction than a feature list.
Developer communities are split on AI-built software. Saying plainly how it was built beats hiding it.
Static pages on Cloudflare are nearly free, so the whole thing runs on free tiers.
If one of them is useful to you, tell me what's missing. That's what I build next.
articles.title: Nine small free things I built in my spare time, and why they live on one page

articles.description:
A parent branch can match its remote exactly while its child still contains an earlier version of that parent. In a stack of GitLab merge requests, that can make the child diff show changes that belong to the parent. This showed up in a local test for GitLab CLI issue #8283. The useful clue was the commit graph hiding behind a perfectly reasonable git status.
This creates a disposable repository and a local bare remote. The lease-protected push below goes to that local directory.
demo=$(mktemp -d)
git init -q --bare "$demo/origin.git"
git init -q -b main "$demo/work"
cd "$demo/work"
git remote add origin ../origin.git
git config user.name "Stack Demo"
git config user.email stack-demo@example.invalid
printf "mode=base\n" > settings.txt
git add settings.txt
git commit -qm "Initial setting"

…

"AI is rotting developers' brains" makes a great headline. The evidence is more interesting than that. There is no proof that using an AI assistant lowers your intelligence. There is a small but growing set of randomized trials suggesting that how you use AI decides whether you learn or just ship.
Here is what the best studies found, where they fall short, and eight habits (plus a tiny script) you can use to keep your skills sharp.
In a randomized trial, experienced open-source developers were 19% slower with AI tools while believing they were faster.
In another randomized trial, developers learning a new library with AI scored 17 points lower on a quiz about code they had just written. The speed gain was not statistically significant.
The people who kept learning used AI to ask conceptual…
